question.text: Scenario: Rohan Sharma is comparing two stocks using relative valuation. Stock X: CMP Rs.500, EPS Rs.25, Expected EPS growth 20%, BV Rs.100, Revenue per share Rs.200, EBITDA per share Rs.50, EV per share Rs.600. Stock Y: CMP Rs.300, EPS Rs.30, Expected EPS growth 10%, BV Rs.150, Revenue per share Rs.250, EBITDA per share Rs.40, EV per share Rs.350. Question 5 of 5: Based on the comprehensive relative valuation, which stock offers better value?

answer.text: Stock X because it has a higher market price
Stock Y appears cheaper on PE, P/BV, and EV/EBITDA, while PEG is equal; lower multiples alone are insufficient because growth, risk, ROE, and quality must also be considered
Neither offers any value as both are overpriced

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the NISM Series XV Research Analyst workbook (pages 207-211), Stock Y looks cheaper on PE (10 vs 20), P/BV (2 vs 5), and EV/EBITDA (8.75 vs 12), while PEG is equal at 1.0 for both stocks. Lower multiples are treated as attractive only "all else equal", and page 208 notes that growth can change the comparison. The Trap: Saying all of Stock Y's multiples are lower overstates the case since PEG is equal; price alone (option A) is not a valuation signal, and labelling both stocks identical (option C) or both overpriced (option D) ignores the multiple-by-multiple gap. Note: Page 213 cautions that relative valuation only gives a sense of cheap vs expensive - confirm any conclusion against growth, risk, ROE, and quality before acting.
